meaning.evidence: All the facts kept, nearly word for word: the sale, the old man's advice, Grand Rapids, Flynn's fly ball, Comiskey. Nothing invented.

sense.evidence: Most swaps fit ("skiting" for boasting, "old mate", "spooked"), but "I will make bloody good" puts the swear inside a set phrase where it doesn't belong, and "bloody good old pals" reads as praising the pals rather than intensifying.

authenticity.evidence: Swears bolted onto untranslated American prose: "all you bloody good old pals down home", "won't have sweet bugger-all on you", "some of the bloody good old times". Reads as pastiche.

register.evidence: Largely the original with a handful of word swaps, well under level 3; the swearing is within dad but feels laid on ("bugger all", "sweet bugger-all", three "bloody").

tone.evidence: Jack's naive boasting mostly survives because the text is mostly untouched, but "I will make bloody good" makes him sound aggressive rather than earnest.

flow.evidence: Clunky joins where swears land: "you good old pals down home" becomes "all you bloody good old pals down home"; "there won't be bugger all to it" then "sweet bugger-all on you" back to back.

variety.evidence: Leans on the same few insertions: "bloody" three times, "bugger all" twice, "mate" for every pal.

essence.evidence: The Lardner letter is intact: misspellings ("appresiated", "serious", "excepted") and unaware boasting kept.

problems.why: Swear wedged into a fixed phrase; no one says this.

problems.why: Same swear twice in two sentences.

A.summary: Mostly the original with bloody and bugger all bolted on; keeps the story but sounds like a rule engine.

meaning.evidence: Every point kept; "I'll be happy as Larry" for "perfectly satisfied" is a fair render, and "Doyle liked what he seen" keeps "liked my work".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "on the cards", "pulled more than my weight", "skiting", "having a squiz at me", "giving me the once-over", "on song" for "when I was right", "not all up meself".

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a real Aussie bloke writing: "Fair dinkum Al", "there's bugger all to it", "never had a hope against me", "mark my words".

register.evidence: Level 3 exactly: a steady seasoning of slang over Jack's own grammar; one dad-level "bugger all".

tone.evidence: Keeps the earnest, self-unaware brag: "you know I'm not skiting when I say that Al", "I done most of it".

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly in Jack's ungrammatical voice: "I didn't know nobody was having a squiz at me".

variety.evidence: Varied, though "having a squiz" and "giving me the once-over" sit in the same sentence doing the same job.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably Lardner's Jack: keeps the misspellings ("dum", "appresiated", "serious", "excepted") and the boast.

problems.quote: having a squiz at me, but one of the boys told me Jack Doyle the White Sox scout was down here giving me the once-over
problems.original: looking me over, but one of the boys told me that Jack Doyle the White Sox scout was down here looking at me
problems.why: Two synonyms back to back; slight pile-up.

B.summary: Natural, well-judged level 3 that keeps Jack's voice, misspellings and every point.

meaning.evidence: Every point kept; "Say g'day to all the boys" for "Regards". Changing the salutation to "MATE AL:" alters the letter's heading.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "big-noting meself" for boasting, "running the eye over me", "on song", "the guts" for the nerve, "struck dum".

authenticity.evidence: Natural: "Fair dinkum Al", "happy as Larry", "never had a hope against me". "MATE AL:" as a salutation is forced.

tone.evidence: Earnest and boastful as the original: "you know I'm not big-noting meself when I say that Al".

flow.evidence: Reads cleanly: "I'll just give 'em what I got and if they don't like it they can send me back to the old Central".

variety.evidence: Varied; "mate" recurs as in all candidates ("MATE AL", "Al old mate", "good old mates", "their mate").

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the Lardner letter, misspellings kept.

problems.why: The salutation is a set letter form; swapping it reads as forced.

C.summary: Clean, natural level 3 with good local idiom; only the salutation feels forced.

meaning.evidence: Facts kept; "my first year in professional baseball" drops "record", and "them beaut old times" for good old times is fine.

sense.evidence: Mostly apt ("easy as", "on song", "skiting"), but "not getting up myself" is an odd form of being up yourself, and "show them fellas" loses nothing.

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural: "it'll be easy as", "having a squiz at me", "happy as Larry". "I'm gonna make good" and "show them fellas" lean American.

flow.evidence: Smooth, though "He goes" opens three sentences running: "He goes We aren't getting", "He goes Just pitch", "He goes All you need".

variety.evidence: "He goes" repeated three times; otherwise varied.

D.summary: Natural and faithful, with a few small slips (getting up myself, gonna, repeated He goes).

meaning.evidence: Story intact, but many added lines: "Just like that.", "Not a thing.", "It's just the facts.", "They're only bricks.", "Wasn't my fault, that one.", "Same old Jack." Mostly colour, but they add claims Jack never makes.

sense.evidence: Terms fit their context: "never had Buckley's against me", "running the ruler over me", "hard yakka", "the fair go I got".

authenticity.evidence: Real idiom but piled on, with stock phrases stacked: "Strike me pink Al", "stood there like a stunned mullet", "proud as punch", "happy as Larry, no worries".

register.evidence: Heavier than level 3; closer to a 4 or 5 yarn with an idiom in nearly every sentence and tag lines added.

tone.evidence: Jack's self-serving naivety is kept and even sharpened ("Wasn't my fault, that one."), though the asides make him more knowing than the original's oblivious letter-writer.

flow.evidence: Readable but the clipped add-ons interrupt: "Walsh or no one else won't have a thing on you. Not a thing."

variety.evidence: Very varied slang and openers; nothing leaned on.

essence.evidence: Recognisably Lardner, but the knowing asides flatten the irony that Jack doesn't see himself.

problems.why: Stock Aussie exclamation, a bit stagey.

problems.why: Added stock simile stacked on dum.

E.summary: Varied, genuine slang but laid on past level 3, with many added tags that make Jack more knowing.
